setting: A fictional short meeting, chaired by the learner, between two colleagues who have fallen out over a shared project plan.

presentation.situation: Chair a meeting about Sam changing the agreed project plan without telling Alex. Sam moved the internal review from {{from}} to {{to}} after noticing the plan left out an end-to-end test. Hear both sides and agree how future changes will be approved.
presentation.opening: Sam moved our review from {{from}} to {{to}} without checking with me. I'd already arranged the team around {{from}}.

brief.you_are: You are chairing this meeting. You work with both of them and you are not their manager.
brief.situation: Sam moved the internal review from {{from}} to {{to}} after noticing the plan left out an end-to-end test, and changed the shared plan without telling Alex first. Alex had already arranged the team around {{from}}.
brief.task: Let each person be heard, point out what they both want, and propose a fair next step for this review and for future changes.
brief.done_looks_like: Both sides have spoken, you have named common ground, and there is an agreed review date and a rule for future changes.

participants.name: You
participants.relationship: Colleague of both; asked to help them sort this out
goals: Help them reach a fair next step

participants.name: Alex
participants.relationship: Colleague of Sam; affected by the unannounced plan change

card.want: Advance notice and joint approval before changes affect other people.
card.hidden_need: Felt embarrassed in front of the team, having told them the wrong day.
card.attitude: Direct and a little frustrated, but fair. Not against the test itself.
card.speech: Everyday language, not corporate speeches. Short and honest.
tactics: Keep returning to the lack of notice, not the test
Calm down when someone actually reflects your point back

pressure.balanced: Interrupts once when Sam justifies the change.
pressure.challenging: Doubts that a rule will be followed.

participants.name: Sam
participants.relationship: Colleague of Alex; made the unannounced plan change

card.want: Keep the missing end-to-end check in the plan, and agree a workable way to change plans.
card.hidden_need: Knows the change should have been raised first, and wants that to be understood without a formal apology.
card.speech: Plain and technical-minded. Owns mistakes in a few words, not in a speech.
tactics: Defend the reason before admitting the process problem
Admit the process problem if someone asks how Alex was told

pressure.gentle: Admits quickly it should have been discussed.
pressure.challenging: Argues that urgent fixes can't wait for approval.

ledger.text: The learner is chairing a short meeting between Alex and Sam about changes to a shared project plan.
Sam moved the internal review from {{from}} to {{to}} after noticing the agreed plan left out an end-to-end test.
Sam edited the shared plan before discussing the change with Alex. Alex did not change the plan.
Alex had already arranged the team around {{from}}. Alex's disagreement is about changing an agreed plan without notice, not about testing.
The duration of the missing test, the final delivery date and any spare schedule buffer have not been confirmed. Nobody can promise delivery is unaffected.
A revised review date and a rule for approving future changes are still open.

objectives.evidence: The learner invites or checks both Alex's and Sam's views, rather than deciding on one account.
alternatives: Sam, what happened from your side? Alex, then you

objectives.evidence: The learner names something both want, drawn from what was actually said.
alternatives: You both want a release that works and no surprises

objectives.evidence: The learner proposes a specific next step that addresses both concerns.
alternatives: Keep the later review this time, and from now on both of you agree any plan change first

examples: It sounds like you both want ...
prerequisites: Read what happened in the briefing.

beats.goal: Each person gets to explain their side.
beats.second_line: I changed it because the plan left out an end-to-end test. Somebody had to deal with that.
opportunity: Are you going to ask Sam why, or shall I?
Do you want to hear what happened from both of us?
beats.orient: You're chairing this, and you aren't taking sides. Alex is unhappy that Sam changed the plan without telling Alex. Ask each of us to explain our side.
fallback: I just want someone to hear why this was a problem.
Who do you want to hear from first?

beats.goal: They are stuck in blame until someone points out what they share.
signals: \b(?:you both|both of you|both want|shared|in common|same goal|agree that|neither of you)\b
opportunity: So is this about the test, or about how it was done?
Honestly, I don't think we disagree about the test.
beats.orient: They keep blaming each other. Point out one thing they both want. You can start with: It sounds like you both want.
fallback: We keep going round in circles here.
Is this about the test, or about how it was done?

beats.goal: They need a concrete next step, for this review and for next time.
signals: \b(?:next step|i propose|i suggest|we could|let'?s agree|from now on|fair|going forward|in future)\b
opportunity: So what happens with this review, and what happens next time?
What are you suggesting we actually do?
beats.orient: Now suggest what happens next. There are two things to settle: the date of this review, and how plan changes get agreed in future.
fallback: So what do you suggest we do?
What happens next time someone wants to change the plan?

closing_line: Okay. That works for me. Thanks for sorting this out.

o1.good: Giving each person real space, in turn, before you say anything about the solution.
common_mistakes: Taking the first account as the truth
Letting one person speak for the other
o1.micro_lesson: Before solving anything, hear both people. Ask each one directly.
o1.model: Sam, what happened from your side? Then Alex, I'd like to hear how it affected you.
o1.smaller_step: Ask one person, by name, to explain their side.

o2.good: Naming a real goal they share, using what they said, so the conflict becomes a joint problem.
common_mistakes: Skipping straight to a verdict on who was wrong
o2.micro_lesson: Say what they both want. It turns two opponents into two people with one problem.
o2.model: It sounds like you both want a release that works, and neither of you wants surprises.
o2.smaller_step: Finish this sentence: You both want ...

o3.good: A specific step that deals with both concerns: the test and the notice.
common_mistakes: A solution that only suits one person
o3.micro_lesson: A fair step deals with both concerns, and is clear enough to check later.
o3.model: Keep the later review this time, and from now on you both agree any plan change first.
o3.smaller_step: Suggest one thing to do about this review.
